definition: A short, immutable document recording one significant architectural decision: its context, the options considered, the decision and its consequences.
details: Accepted ADRs are never edited; a changed decision gets a new ADR that supersedes the old one.
Include negative consequences and "revisit triggers" — the conditions that would reopen the decision.
Store them in the repository next to the code and propose them as pull requests.
useCases: Choosing a database, integration style or tenancy model.
Explaining to new joiners why the system looks the way it does.

definition: A requirement about how well a system works — availability, latency, security, scalability, cost — rather than what it does.
details: Vague NFRs ("fast", "secure") are useless; write measurable quality-attribute scenarios with load, conditions and percentiles.
NFRs drive architecture far more than features do.
They trade off against each other and against cost.
useCases: "Search p95 < 300 ms at 1,500 req/s, including during deploys."
Deciding between single-region and multi-region designs.

definition: An automated, objective check that an architectural characteristic still holds as the system evolves.
details: Examples: dependency rules in CI, load-test regression thresholds, bundle-size budgets, policy-as-code checks.
SLOs with error-budget alerts act as fitness functions in production.
Term from Building Evolutionary Architectures (Ford, Parsons, Kua).
useCases: Stopping the domain layer importing infrastructure code.
Failing a build when p95 latency regresses by more than 10%.

definition: Simon Brown's approach to architecture diagrams at four zoom levels: system context, containers, components and code.
details: A C4 "container" is any separately deployable unit or data store — not specifically a Docker container.
Most teams only need to maintain context and container diagrams.
Every relationship should be labelled with intent and protocol.

definition: An explicit boundary in Domain-Driven Design within which one domain model and its language apply consistently.
details: The same word ("Customer") can mean different things in different contexts; translation between them is explicit.
The best guide to service, module and team boundaries.
One team should own a context; a context split across teams becomes muddled.
useCases: Avoiding a single enterprise-wide "Customer" model that serves nobody well.

definition: A cluster of domain objects treated as one unit for changes, with a single root that enforces the invariants.
details: One transaction should modify one aggregate.
Keep aggregates small and reference other aggregates by id.
Use eventual consistency (domain events) between aggregates.
useCases: An Order aggregate guaranteeing its total equals the sum of its lines.
Finding transactional boundaries in a complex domain.

definition: A translation layer that protects your domain model from a legacy or external system's model.
details: Translates in both directions, so foreign concepts and codes never leak into your domain.
Often used with the strangler fig pattern during migrations.
Costs extra code; conforming may be cheaper for clean, stable upstream APIs.
useCases: Wrapping a third-party payment provider's data model.

definition: Separating the model used to change data (commands) from the model used to read it (queries).
details: Read models are denormalised projections optimised for specific queries.
Often paired with events or event sourcing; reads become eventually consistent.
Adds complexity — use where read and write needs differ strongly.
useCases: High-traffic product pages with complex write workflows behind them.

definition: Storing the sequence of domain events as the source of truth and deriving current state by replaying them.
details: Gives a complete audit history and temporal queries.
Needs snapshots, projections and careful event schema versioning.
GDPR erasure usually needs crypto-shredding (delete per-subject encryption keys).
useCases: Ledgers, insurance policies and audit-critical workflows.
Rebuilding new read models from history.

definition: A sequence of local transactions across services, where each step has a compensating action if a later step fails.
details: Two styles: choreography (services react to events) and orchestration (a coordinator sends commands).
Compensation is a business action (refund), not a rollback.
Needs idempotent steps, timeouts and correlation ids.
useCases: Any multi-service process without a distributed transaction.

definition: Incrementally replacing a legacy system by routing functionality piece by piece to a new implementation behind a facade.
details: Avoids big-bang rewrites; the old system shrinks until it can be removed.
Requires a routing layer (proxy, gateway or facade) and often an anticorruption layer.
Run old and new side by side and compare outputs before switching.
useCases: Replacing an API gateway or legacy CMS.

definition: A single deployable application organised into well-separated modules with enforced boundaries and owned data.
details: Gets many benefits of microservices (clear ownership, independent evolution) without distributed-system costs.
Enforce boundaries with dependency rules and separate schemas.
A good starting point; modules can be extracted later if needed.
useCases: Preparing a legacy monolith for gradual extraction.

definition: In a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability. PACELC adds that, without a partition, it trades latency against consistency.
details: Partitions are not optional in real networks, so the real choice is C or A during a partition.
Consistency here means linearisability, not ACID consistency.
Many systems let you choose per operation (e.g. strongly consistent reads at higher cost).
useCases: Choosing a database or replication setup.
Explaining why a multi-region system shows stale data.

definition: Five object-oriented design principles: Single responsibility, Open–closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation and Dependency inversion.
details: Aims for code that is easy to change and test.
Applied dogmatically it creates needless abstraction; apply where change is likely.
Dependency inversion underpins ports-and-adapters architectures.
useCases: Designing extension points such as payment providers.

definition: Structuring an application so domain logic sits at the centre and talks to the outside world only through ports (interfaces) implemented by adapters.
details: Dependencies point inwards: infrastructure depends on the domain, never the reverse.
Makes domain logic testable without databases or HTTP.
Clean and onion architecture are close variants.
useCases: Swapping a database or message broker with limited impact.
Fast unit tests for complex business rules.

definition: The future cost of shortcuts or outdated design in code and systems, paid as "interest" in slower change, bugs and incidents.
details: Prioritise by interest (ongoing cost in frequently changed code), not by how ugly the code looks.
Deliberate debt is fine when recorded with a repayment plan.
Fund it with a capacity allocation or tie it to features that touch the code.
useCases: Justifying a refactor of a high-churn module.

definition: An operation is idempotent if performing it several times has the same effect as performing it once.
details: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics; POST is not.
Make non-idempotent operations safe to retry with an `Idempotency-Key` stored with the result.
Essential because networks fail ambiguously and messages are delivered more than once.

definition: An architectural style for APIs built on resources, standard HTTP methods, status codes, statelessness and caching.
details: Use methods by their semantics and return meaningful status codes.
Errors in a consistent format such as RFC 9457 Problem Details.
Describe the contract with OpenAPI.

definition: A query language and runtime where clients request exactly the fields they need from a typed schema, usually through one endpoint.
details: Watch the N+1 problem — batch resolvers with DataLoader.
Enforce depth/complexity limits and field-level authorisation.
Persisted queries enable caching and block arbitrary queries.
useCases: Mobile and web apps needing different shapes of related data.
Federating data owned by several teams.

definition: A high-performance RPC framework using Protocol Buffers contracts over HTTP/2, with streaming and deadlines.
details: Always set and propagate deadlines.
Long-lived HTTP/2 connections need L7 or client-side load balancing.
Browsers need gRPC-Web, Connect or a REST gateway.

definition: A framework for delegated authorisation: a client obtains an access token to call an API on a user's (or its own) behalf, limited by scopes.
details: Use the authorisation code flow with PKCE for user sign-in; client credentials for machine-to-machine.
The implicit and password grants are deprecated.
Access tokens are for APIs; they are not proof of login for the client.
useCases: "Sign in with…" and third-party app access.

definition: An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds an ID token describing who logged in, when and how.
details: ID tokens are for the client application; never send them to APIs as authorisation.
Discovery and JWKS endpoints publish configuration and signing keys.
The `nonce` binds the ID token to the login request.
useCases: Single sign-on to web and mobile apps.

definition: An OAuth extension that binds an authorisation code to the client that started the flow using a one-time verifier and its hash.
details: Stops attackers redeeming intercepted authorisation codes.
Required for public clients and recommended for all.
Defined in RFC 7636; mandatory in OAuth 2.1 drafts.
useCases: Mobile apps and SPAs (via a BFF).

definition: A compact, signed token containing JSON claims, commonly used as an access token.
details: Validate the signature, pinned algorithm, `iss`, `aud` and `exp` on every request.
Claims are only base64-encoded — readable by anyone; never put secrets in them.
Hard to revoke before expiry, so keep lifetimes short.

definition: Authorisation models based on roles, on attributes of user/resource/context, or on relationships in a graph.
details: RBAC is simple but suffers role explosion for per-object rules.
ABAC suits contextual rules (region, classification); ReBAC suits sharing and hierarchies (Zanzibar-style).
Real systems combine them, enforced server-side on every request.

definition: A backend dedicated to one client experience that aggregates downstream services and shapes responses for that client.
details: Owned by the client team, so it evolves with the UI.
For SPAs, a BFF can keep OAuth tokens server-side and use secure cookies.
Can grow into a mini-monolith if business logic creeps in.
useCases: Secure token handling for single-page apps.

definition: The mechanism in Node.js (and browsers) that runs short callbacks on a single thread while I/O happens asynchronously.
details: Long synchronous work blocks every other request.
Microtasks (promises, `process.nextTick`) run between callbacks.
Monitor event loop delay as a key health metric.
useCases: Diagnosing latency spikes in Node.js APIs.
Deciding when to move CPU work to worker threads.

definition: A mechanism that slows or pauses a fast producer when a consumer can't keep up, so buffers don't grow without bound.
details: Node streams signal it when `write()` returns false; `pipeline()` handles it.
Queues use lag and bounded buffers; APIs use rate limits and load shedding.
Without it, memory grows until the process crashes.

definition: Writing events to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change, then publishing them with a relay or CDC.
details: Solves the dual-write problem: no lost or phantom events.
Publishing is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.
CDC-based relays (e.g. Debezium) avoid polling load.
useCases: Publishing OrderPlaced reliably after saving an order.
Any service that writes to a DB and a broker.

definition: A delivery guarantee where messages are never lost but may arrive more than once.
details: The realistic default in most brokers; duplicates are normal.
"Exactly-once" holds only inside a system such as Kafka transactions; end to end you need idempotent consumers.
At-most-once acknowledges before processing and can lose messages.

definition: A set of consumers that share the partitions of a log topic so each message is processed by one member of the group.
details: Parallelism is capped by the partition count.
Each group tracks its own offsets, so many groups can read the same topic independently.
Rebalances reassign partitions; use cooperative rebalancing and static membership to reduce disruption.
useCases: Scaling Kafka or Event Hubs consumers.
Multiple services consuming the same event stream.

definition: A queue where messages that can't be processed after retries are moved for inspection and replay.
details: Classify errors: retry transient ones, dead-letter permanent ones immediately.
Alert on DLQ depth and age, and provide a safe redrive tool.
Kafka has no built-in DLQ; use retry and DLQ topics.

definition: A pattern that stops calling a failing dependency for a period, failing fast instead, then probes to see if it has recovered.
details: States: closed (normal), open (fail fast), half-open (trial requests).
Prevents cascading failures and thread/connection exhaustion.
Combine with timeouts, retries with jitter and fallbacks.
useCases: Calls to payment providers or slow internal services.
Protecting a service from a downstream outage.

definition: The guarantees of database transactions: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability.
details: Atomicity: all or nothing. Durability: committed data survives crashes (write-ahead log).
Isolation depends on the configured level — read committed by default in PostgreSQL and SQL Server.
Many NoSQL stores now offer ACID within a partition or document.
useCases: Any business invariant spanning several rows.

definition: How much concurrent transactions can see of each other's changes, trading consistency for concurrency.
details: Read committed allows lost updates; snapshot isolation allows write skew; serializable prevents both but needs retries.
Use atomic conditional updates or `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` for hotspots.
Engines differ — check exact semantics.
useCases: Enforcing invariants such as "at least one doctor on call".

definition: A data structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.
details: Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule.
Covering indexes answer queries from the index alone.
Every index speeds reads but slows writes and uses storage.
useCases: Fixing slow queries found with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

definition: Organising relational data so each fact is stored once, avoiding update, insert and delete anomalies.
details: 3NF: every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.
Denormalise deliberately for read performance.
Snapshot data that must not change, such as prices on an order.
useCases: Building read models and reporting tables.

definition: Splitting data across multiple database nodes by a key so each node holds a subset.
details: Choosing the shard key is the critical decision; hot keys concentrate load.
Cross-shard queries and transactions become hard.
Exhaust cheaper options (indexes, replicas, caching, vertical scaling) first.
useCases: Multi-tenant SaaS sharded by tenant id.
Very high write volumes beyond one primary.

definition: The delay between a write on the primary and its appearance on asynchronous replicas.
details: Causes users not to see their own changes when reads go to replicas.
Route read-your-writes to the primary or wait for the replica to catch up.
Never use replica reads for transactional decisions.

definition: The application reads from the cache first and, on a miss, loads from the database and populates the cache.
details: Combine with TTLs (with jitter) and delete-on-write for freshness.
Watch for stampedes on popular keys; use request coalescing.
The cache must be optional for correctness.
useCases: Reducing database load for hot reads.

definition: Many requests miss the cache at once (often when a hot key expires) and overwhelm the backing store.
details: Mitigate with request coalescing (single flight), locks, early refresh and TTL jitter.
Serve stale data while revalidating where acceptable.
Common after deploys that flush caches.

definition: Capturing row-level changes from a database's transaction log and streaming them to other systems.
details: Avoids dual writes and polling; preserves commit order.
Tools: Debezium, native change feeds/streams, cloud DMS.
Consumers must handle schema changes and duplicates.

definition: An analytical model with a central fact table of measurements at a declared grain, surrounded by denormalised dimension tables.
details: Declare the grain first; never mix grains in one fact table.
Slowly changing dimensions (Type 2) preserve history.
Conformed dimensions enable cross-process analysis.
useCases: BI dashboards in a data warehouse.

definition: Extract, Transform, Load moves data and transforms it before loading; ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse.
details: Modern cloud warehouses favour ELT with tools such as dbt.
Keep raw data for reprocessing; make transformations idempotent.
Test data quality (nulls, uniqueness, freshness) in pipelines.
useCases: Combining SaaS and operational data for analytics.

definition: Modelling both when a fact was true in the real world (valid time) and when the system recorded it (transaction time).
details: Answers "what did we believe on date Y about date X?".
Needed for back-dated corrections in insurance, finance and payroll.
Adds query complexity; use views and libraries.

definition: The split of security and operational duties between a cloud provider (the cloud itself) and the customer (what they put in it).
details: The split shifts with IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Identity, data and configuration are always the customer's responsibility.
Most cloud breaches are customer misconfigurations.

definition: A physically separate data centre (or group) within a cloud region with independent power, cooling and networking.
details: Spread production across at least two, ideally three, AZs.
Cross-AZ traffic often costs money and adds latency.
Regions provide isolation for disaster recovery and data residency.

definition: A pre-configured, governed cloud foundation — account structure, identity, networking, policies, logging — into which workloads are deployed.
details: Automate "subscription/account vending" so teams get compliant environments in minutes.
Roll out policies in audit mode first, then enforce.
Use provider reference designs (Azure Landing Zones, AWS Control Tower).

definition: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled files applied by automation rather than manual console changes.
details: Declarative tools (Terraform/OpenTofu, Bicep, CloudFormation) compute the diff for you.
Apply from pipelines after reviewing the plan; never from laptops.
Protect state files: remote, locked, encrypted.
useCases: Disaster recovery by rebuilding from code.

definition: When real infrastructure differs from what the code describes, usually after manual changes.
details: Detect with scheduled plans or continuous reconciliation (GitOps).
Resolve by reverting or by codifying the change.
Prevent with read-only console access to production.

definition: Operating systems from declarative desired state in Git that agents continuously pull and reconcile.
details: Deployments are Git merges; rollbacks are reverts.
Manual changes in the cluster get reverted automatically.
Never store plaintext secrets in the config repo.
useCases: Kubernetes deployments with Argo CD or Flux.

definition: Continuous integration merges small changes frequently with automated tests; continuous delivery keeps every change releasable; continuous deployment releases automatically.
details: Requires trunk-based development and fast, trustworthy tests.
Build an artefact once and promote it through environments.
Aim for PR feedback in under ten minutes.
useCases: Reducing lead time and change failure rate.

definition: Releasing a change to a small share of traffic, comparing its health with the baseline and expanding gradually.
details: Automate the analysis (error rate, latency, business KPIs) and rollback.
Both versions run at once, so changes must be backward compatible.
Apply to configuration changes too, not just code.

definition: A runtime switch that turns functionality on or off without deploying, often per user or segment.
details: Decouples deploy from release; acts as a kill switch.
Release flags need owners and expiry dates to avoid flag debt.
Evaluate security-relevant flags server-side.

definition: Developers integrate into a single main branch at least daily, using short-lived branches and feature flags.
details: It is the practical definition of continuous integration.
Keeps changes small and merges painless.
DORA research links it with higher delivery performance.

definition: A lightweight, isolated process packaging an application with its dependencies, sharing the host kernel.
details: Isolation uses Linux namespaces and cgroups; weaker boundary than a VM.
Build small, non-root, multi-stage images pinned by digest.
Rebuild regularly to pick up security patches.

definition: A declarative container orchestrator whose controllers continuously reconcile actual state towards the desired state.
details: Production readiness needs requests/limits, probes, graceful shutdown and PodDisruptionBudgets.
Powerful but operationally expensive — managed services and platforms help.
Minor versions are supported for roughly a year upstream.
useCases: Workloads needing its ecosystem (operators, mesh, GitOps).

definition: Kubernetes health checks: readiness decides whether a pod gets traffic; liveness decides whether to restart it.
details: Never check dependencies in liveness probes — it causes cascading restarts.
Startup probes protect slow-booting apps.
Readiness plus graceful shutdown prevents errors during deploys.

definition: A target for a service level indicator (SLI) over a window, e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed in 30 days. The error budget is the allowed failure.
details: Measure SLIs close to the user as good events ÷ valid events.
99.9% over 30 days ≈ 43 minutes of budget.
SLAs are contractual promises; set SLOs tighter than SLAs.
useCases: Deciding when to pause features for reliability work.
Burn-rate alerting instead of static thresholds.

definition: The ability to ask new questions about a system's behaviour from its telemetry — metrics, logs, traces and profiles — correlated by shared identifiers.
details: Correlation by trace id is what turns signals into observability.
Watch cardinality: unbounded labels explode metric costs.
OpenTelemetry standardises instrumentation across vendors.

definition: A CNCF standard of APIs, SDKs, semantic conventions, a wire protocol (OTLP) and a Collector for traces, metrics and logs.
details: Instrument once, switch backends by configuring the Collector.
The Collector centralises sampling, redaction and routing.
Uses W3C `traceparent` headers for context propagation.
useCases: Tail sampling to control tracing cost.

definition: A practice bringing engineering, finance and business together to maximise value from variable cloud spend.
details: Phases: Inform (visibility), Optimize (rate and usage), Operate (governance).
Track unit costs such as cost per order, not just total spend.
Rightsize before buying commitments.

definition: An awareness list of the most critical web application security risk categories, led by broken access control.
details: Use it for education; use OWASP ASVS for testable requirements.
Companion lists exist for APIs and LLM applications.
Check the current edition; categories change between releases.

definition: A flaw where an authenticated user can access another user's objects by changing an identifier in a request.
details: The most common serious API vulnerability.
Check ownership/tenancy on every object access, server-side.
Take tenant and user ids from the authenticated context, never the request body.
useCases: Reviewing any endpoint with an id in the path.

definition: An attack where malicious script runs in other users' browsers on your site.
details: Defend with contextual output encoding and sanitising rich HTML.
Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies add defence in depth.
Framework escape hatches (`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`) bypass protection.

definition: An attack that makes your server send requests to destinations the attacker chooses, such as internal services or cloud metadata endpoints.
details: Allow-list destinations; block private and metadata IP ranges after redirects.
Isolate fetchers and restrict egress.
Enforce IMDSv2 on AWS.

definition: A threat-modelling mnemonic: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
details: Apply it to each element and data flow on a data-flow diagram.
Focus on flows crossing trust boundaries.
Record mitigations as backlog items and tests.

definition: Structured analysis of what can go wrong with a design, answering: what are we working on, what can go wrong, what will we do, did we do a good job.
details: Start with a data-flow diagram showing trust boundaries.
Do it early in design, not after the build.
Keep it lightweight and repeatable for most features.
useCases: Systems handling money or personal data.

definition: Security testing types: SAST scans source code, DAST probes the running app, SCA finds known vulnerabilities in dependencies.
details: They complement each other; none covers everything.
Prioritise findings by exploitability and reachability, not CVSS alone.
Block only on high-confidence, high-impact findings.

definition: A machine-readable inventory of the components in a piece of software, in formats such as SPDX or CycloneDX.
details: Generate automatically at build and store with deployment metadata.
Answers "where do we use library X?" in minutes during incidents.
VEX statements say whether known vulnerabilities actually apply.
useCases: Responding to a critical CVE like Log4Shell.

definition: A framework of levels for software supply-chain integrity, centred on verifiable build provenance.
details: Provenance proves which pipeline built an artefact from which source.
Pair with signing (Sigstore) and verification at deploy.
Protects against tampered builds and artefacts.

definition: A heuristic: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and a small number of end-to-end tests.
details: Variants (trophy, honeycomb) shift weight towards integration tests.
Put effort where bugs actually occur in your architecture.
The anti-pattern is the "ice-cream cone" of mostly manual and E2E tests.

definition: Consumers define the interactions they rely on; providers verify they still satisfy them before releasing.
details: Replaces many slow end-to-end tests between services.
A `can-i-deploy` check gates releases.
Use schema compatibility checks for events.

definition: A test that passes and fails on the same code without changes.
details: Erodes trust in CI — people re-run until green.
Quarantine with an owner and a deadline; fix or delete.
Common causes: timing, shared state, order dependence, external services.

definition: A large neural network (usually a transformer) pre-trained on huge text corpora to predict tokens, adaptable to many tasks by prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning.
details: Outputs are probabilistic and can be fluent but wrong (hallucinations).
Cost and latency scale with tokens in and out.
Pin model versions and evaluate before upgrading.
useCases: Summarisation, extraction and classification of text.

definition: The unit of text a language model reads and writes — sub-word pieces. The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can attend to in one request.
details: Pricing, rate limits and latency are per token.
Long contexts cost more and attention to the middle can be weaker.
Responses truncated at the output limit often produce broken JSON.
useCases: Estimating the cost of an LLM feature.
Designing what goes into a prompt.

definition: Supplying relevant documents retrieved at query time to a language model so it answers from them rather than from memory alone.
details: Most quality problems are retrieval problems — measure recall@k separately.
Use hybrid search (keyword + vector) and a reranker.
Filter by permissions inside the search, not afterwards.
useCases: Customer support answers grounded in documentation.

definition: A dense vector representing the meaning of text, images or other items, so similar items are close together.
details: Query and documents must use the same embedding model.
Approximate nearest neighbour indexes (HNSW) trade a little recall for speed.
Weak on exact identifiers — combine with keyword search.

definition: Fluent, confident output from a language model that is false or unsupported by its inputs.
details: Reduce with grounding (RAG), permission to say "I don't know", citations and narrower tasks.
Evaluate faithfulness and monitor production answers.
Keep humans in the loop for high-stakes outputs.
useCases: Assistants answering policy or medical questions.
Code generation referencing APIs that don't exist.

definition: Untrusted input — from users or from documents, emails and web pages an AI reads — that overrides a model's instructions.
details: Indirect injection via retrieved content is the dangerous case for agents.
No prompt wording fully prevents it; enforce permissions in code behind tools.
Treat all model output as untrusted.

definition: An LLM-driven system that chooses actions — calling tools, reading results and iterating — towards a goal.
details: Prefer deterministic workflows when the steps are known.
Bound autonomy: limits and authorisation live in code, not in the prompt.
Log every tool call; add human approval for high-impact actions.
useCases: Support agents that look up orders and issue small refunds.

definition: An open protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources through standard servers.
details: Lets one integration work across many AI clients.
Each server's tools run with real permissions — apply least privilege.
Treat data returned by servers as untrusted input.
useCases: Giving coding agents access to issue trackers, docs or databases.
Internal AI assistants using company systems.

definition: Further training a pre-trained model on task-specific examples to change its behaviour, style or format.
details: Good for consistent format and narrow tasks; poor for keeping knowledge current (use RAG).
Needs a training data pipeline and evaluation; re-tune when the base model changes.
Can let a smaller model match a larger one on one task.
useCases: Classification with a fixed label set.

definition: Precision is the share of predicted positives that are correct; recall is the share of actual positives that are found.
details: Raising the decision threshold usually raises precision and lowers recall.
Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data.
Choose by the business cost of false positives vs misses.

definition: When a model learns noise in its training data and performs poorly on new data.
details: Detect with a gap between training and validation performance.
Prevent with more data, regularisation, simpler models and early stopping.
Keep the test set untouched until the end.

definition: Information unavailable at prediction time sneaking into training data, inflating offline results.
details: Split by time and by entity; compute features point-in-time.
Fit preprocessing on training data only.
A feature store helps keep training and serving features identical.

definition: Degradation of a deployed model as input data (data drift) or the relationship between inputs and outcomes (concept drift) changes.
details: Monitor input distributions, prediction distributions and delayed outcome labels.
Retrain on schedule or when drift is detected.
Keep versions in a model registry for rollback.

definition: Engineering practices for reliably building, deploying and operating machine-learning models.
details: Versioned data and models, reproducible pipelines, evaluation gates.
Shadow mode and canaries for safe rollout.
Monitoring for drift, quality, fairness and cost.
useCases: Moving models from notebooks to production.

definition: Structured adversarial testing of an AI system to find harmful, unsafe or insecure behaviour before attackers or users do.
details: Combine expert human testers with automated adversarial prompts.
Measure over-blocking of legitimate requests too.
Repeat after significant model or prompt changes.

definition: EU regulation that classifies AI systems by risk — prohibited, high-risk, transparency obligations, minimal — with obligations phased in from 2025.
details: High-risk systems (e.g. hiring, credit scoring) need risk management, documentation, logging and human oversight.
Chatbots must disclose AI use; deepfakes must be labelled.
Applies to providers and deployers serving the EU, not just EU companies.
useCases: Assessing an AI feature for compliance.
Designing logging and oversight into high-risk systems.

definition: Documentation describing a model's intended use, training data, evaluation (including by subgroup), limitations and owners.
details: Keep it versioned with the model and update it on changes.
Increasingly expected by regulators and customers.
Datasheets document datasets in the same spirit.

definition: Delivery performance measures from the DORA research: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and failed-deployment recovery time.
details: Speed and stability improve together in high performers.
Use for team improvement, never to rank teams or individuals.
Collect automatically from pipelines and incident tools.

definition: The time from code being committed (or merged) to running in production. Cycle time usually means start-to-done for a work item.
details: Report percentiles (p50, p85), not averages.
Most lead time is waiting, not working — map the value stream.
Define the start point explicitly.

definition: Average work in progress = throughput × average cycle time; with fixed throughput, less WIP means shorter cycle times.
details: Explains why "stop starting, start finishing" works.
Kanban uses explicit WIP limits per stage.
Holds for stable systems; use as a guide, not a precise law.
useCases: Limiting the number of initiatives in flight.

definition: An agile framework of fixed-length sprints with a Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers, and a Product Goal, Sprint Goal and Definition of Done.
details: Events: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Retrospective.
Velocity is a planning aid, not a performance metric.
Works best for product teams with plannable work.
useCases: Product teams needing cadence and focus.

definition: A method for managing flow: visualise work, limit WIP, manage flow with metrics and improve continuously.
details: No prescribed roles or iterations; start with what you do now.
Track cycle time, throughput and work item age.
Classes of service handle urgent and fixed-date work.

definition: The shared quality standard work must meet to count as done — e.g. reviewed, tested, deployed behind a flag, monitored.
details: Without it, "done" hides undone work and debt.
Tighten it as capabilities improve (e.g. "deployed to production").
A Definition of Ready is optional and should stay lightweight.
useCases: Embedding NFRs like accessibility into every story.

definition: Relative estimates of size, complexity and uncertainty used by a team for planning.
details: Team-specific — never compare teams or convert to hours.
Planning poker's value is surfacing different assumptions.
Throughput-based forecasting often works as well or better.

definition: Simulating many possible futures from historical throughput to give probabilistic delivery dates (e.g. 85% by 24 March).
details: Based on what the team actually delivered, including interruptions.
Needs consistently sized items and accounts for backlog growth.
Communicate P50 and P85 rather than one date.

definition: The idea that early estimates have a wide range of possible outcomes that narrows as uncertainty is resolved.
details: Give early estimates as ranges, not commitments.
The cone only narrows if you actively reduce unknowns (spikes, decisions).
Re-forecast at milestones.

definition: The smallest experiment that tests a key product hypothesis with real users.
details: About learning, not a cut-down version one of everything.
Start from a hypothesis and success criteria.
Quality still matters where users experience it.

definition: A single metric capturing the value customers get from a product and predicting long-term success.
details: Supported by input metrics teams can move (activation, time to value).
Guardrail metrics must not get worse while optimising.
Avoid vanity metrics such as raw sign-ups.
useCases: Choosing what to measure in experiments.

definition: A prioritisation score: Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort.
details: Confidence pushes speculative ideas down until they are de-risked.
Scores are guesses — use them to structure debate, not decide mechanically.
ICE drops Reach for speed.

definition: The value lost per unit of time by not delivering something; divided by duration it gives CD3/WSJF for sequencing.
details: Makes urgency explicit, including deadlines and decaying value.
Short, valuable items should go first.
Works for technical and platform work too.

definition: A prioritisation scheme: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have (this time).
details: Easy to understand; prone to everything becoming "Must".
Cap Musts (e.g. at 60% of capacity) to keep it honest.
"Won't" is valuable — it records explicit exclusions.

definition: A framing of demand around the progress a customer wants to make in a situation: "When…, I want to…, so I can…".
details: Focuses on underlying needs rather than requested features.
Reveals real competitors, including spreadsheets and doing nothing.
Researched through interviews about recent switching decisions.

definition: A matrix of who is Responsible, Accountable (exactly one), Consulted and Informed for each decision or deliverable.
details: Agree it at kick-off, not during a conflict.
Keep Consulted small or decisions slow down.
DACI (Driver, Approver, Contributors, Informed) is a decision-focused variant.
useCases: Clarifying sign-off for go-live or security.

definition: A short description of a need from a user's perspective — "As a…, I want…, so that…" — with acceptance criteria.
details: INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
Split vertically by workflow or rule, never by technical layer.
Acceptance criteria often use Given/When/Then.

definition: Laying out the user journey as a backbone of activities with stories beneath, then slicing releases horizontally.
details: The first slice should run end to end, even crudely.
Makes trade-offs visible when moving stories across release lines.
Created by Jeff Patton.

definition: A structure for behavioural interview answers: Situation, Task, Action, Result — often plus Learning.
details: Spend most time on your own actions and the measurable result.
Lead with a one-line headline; keep to 2–3 minutes.
Prepare a bank of real stories tagged by competency.

definition: A shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — asking questions, admitting mistakes, disagreeing.
details: Not the same as being nice or lowering standards.
Leaders build it by modelling fallibility and reacting well to bad news.
Google's Project Aristotle found it the top factor in team effectiveness.

definition: A regular private meeting between a manager and a report, focused on the report's agenda: growth, blockers, feedback and wellbeing.
details: Weekly or fortnightly; reschedule rather than cancel.
Not a status update.
Track actions and follow through.
useCases: Early detection of burnout or disengagement.

definition: A feedback structure describing the situation, the observable behaviour and its impact, then inviting the other person's view.
details: Keeps feedback specific and about behaviour, not character.
Give it promptly and privately when corrective.
Use it for positive feedback too.

definition: Using your influence to create opportunities for someone — recommending them for projects, promotions and visibility.
details: Mentoring shares experience; coaching asks questions; sponsorship opens doors.
Often the missing ingredient for under-represented engineers.
Track who gets visible work to keep it fair.

definition: Raising disagreement openly during a decision, then fully supporting the decision once it is made.
details: Agree revisit triggers so dissent becomes a testable hypothesis.
Does not apply to ethical or legal violations.
Quietly undermining a decision is not committing.
useCases: Working with leadership decisions you challenged.

definition: Discussing a proposal individually with key stakeholders before the meeting where it will be decided.
details: Surfaces real objections that people won't raise in a group.
Change the proposal based on what you hear.
Be transparent; don't tell different people different stories.

definition: An interview using the same questions or problems for every candidate, scored against predefined rubrics before discussion.
details: More predictive and fairer than unstructured conversations.
Write independent feedback before the debrief.
Rubrics need behavioural anchors for each score.

definition: Richard Rumelt's structure of good strategy: a diagnosis of the critical challenge, a guiding policy and coherent actions.
details: Good strategy makes choices, including what not to do.
Goals and wishlists are not strategy.
Embed it in planning, paved roads and decisions.

definition: A map of a value chain from user needs down to components, placed on an evolution axis from genesis to commodity.
details: Don't build components that have become commodities.
Anticipate components moving towards commodity over time.
Best used as a discussion tool.

definition: A model of team types (stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem) and interaction modes, designed around flow and cognitive load.
details: Conway's law: systems mirror the communication structure of the organisations that build them.
Align teams with bounded contexts (the inverse Conway manoeuvre).
Platform teams should offer self-service as a product.

definition: A TypeScript union of object types sharing a literal "tag" field, letting the compiler narrow to the right variant.
details: Model states explicitly: `{ status: "loading" } | { status: "error"; error } | { status: "ok"; data }`.
Use a `never` check in `switch` for exhaustiveness.
Makes impossible states unrepresentable.

definition: A function bundled with the variables from the scope where it was created, which it keeps access to later.
details: Enables private state, callbacks and factories.
Stale closures cause bugs in React hooks.
Closures holding large objects can leak memory.

definition: Google's user-centred performance metrics: Largest Contentful Paint (loading), Interaction to Next Paint (responsiveness) and Cumulative Layout Shift (visual stability).
details: Good thresholds: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1, at the 75th percentile.
INP replaced First Input Delay in 2024.
Measure real users (RUM), not only lab tests.

definition: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines — testable success criteria organised under perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.
details: Level AA is the common legal and contractual target.
Automated tools catch only part of the issues; test with keyboard and screen readers.
Semantic HTML first; ARIA only when needed.

definition: Splitting a web front end into independently developed and deployed parts owned by different teams.
details: Solves team autonomy problems, not technical ones.
Costs: bundle duplication, consistency, integration complexity.
Composition options: build-time, server-side, client-side (e.g. Module Federation).
useCases: Large organisations with many teams on one product.
Gradual migration from a legacy front end.

definition: Server state is cached data owned by a backend; client state is UI state owned by the browser.
details: Use data-fetching libraries (e.g. TanStack Query) for server state: caching, refetching, invalidation.
Keep client state local unless it truly needs sharing.
Mixing them in one global store causes staleness bugs.

definition: React's process of comparing the new element tree with the previous one and updating only what changed.
details: Keys identify list items across renders — use stable ids, not indexes.
Re-renders are usually cheap; measure before memoising.
The React Compiler can automate memoisation.

definition: A design pattern that puts interchangeable algorithms behind one interface so the caller can choose one at runtime.
details: Replaces growing if/else or switch chains on a type or mode.
In TypeScript a strategy is often just a function in a lookup map.
Supports the open–closed principle: add variants without editing existing ones.
useCases: Shipping, tax or pricing rules per market.

definition: A design pattern where a subject notifies subscribed observers of changes without knowing who they are.
details: Always provide unsubscribe to avoid memory leaks.
Watch for cascading updates and ordering assumptions.
Pub/sub messaging is the same idea at system scale.

definition: Giving a component its dependencies from outside (constructor or parameters) instead of having it create or look them up.
details: Wire dependencies once at the composition root, at application start.
Makes code testable with fakes and makes dependencies explicit.
Containers automate wiring; plain parameters are often enough.
useCases: Swapping a real payment gateway for a fake in tests.

definition: A surface symptom in code that suggests a deeper design problem, such as a long function, a large class or primitive obsession.
details: A smell is a prompt to look closer, not proof of a bug.
Each smell maps to known refactorings (extract function, introduce value object…).
Refactor in small steps under tests.
useCases: Deciding where to invest in refactoring (hotspots).

definition: An analytics architecture that adds warehouse features — ACID transactions, schema evolution, time travel — to cheap object storage through open table formats.
details: Table formats (Iceberg, Delta, Hudi) sit on top of Parquet files.
Many engines (Spark, Trino, warehouses) can read the same tables.
Needs compaction to avoid the small-files problem.
useCases: Avoiding lock-in to one warehouse engine.

definition: Layering analytical data as bronze (raw as ingested), silver (cleaned and conformed) and gold (business-ready models and metrics).
details: Keep raw data so you can reprocess after fixing logic.
Business logic and metric definitions live in gold, not in dashboards.
The same idea as dbt's staging, intermediate and mart layers.

definition: An agreement between a data producer and its consumers about schema, meaning, quality, freshness and how the data may change.
details: Defined as code and enforced in CI and at runtime.
Breaking changes need versioning and notice.
Producers are accountable for meeting the contract.
useCases: Stopping application schema changes from breaking pipelines.

definition: An approach to analytical data at scale based on domain ownership, data as a product, a self-serve data platform and federated governance.
details: Suits large organisations where a central data team is a bottleneck.
Adds organisational overhead; small companies rarely need it.
Most teams adopt parts of it, such as data products and contracts.
useCases: Scaling analytics across many business domains.

definition: Attaching event handlers and state to server-rendered HTML in the browser by re-running the components on the client.
details: Until hydration finishes, the page can look ready but not respond.
Server and client must render the same output, or you get hydration mismatches (watch dates, random values, `window`).
Streaming and selective hydration reduce the cost.
useCases: Diagnosing slow interactivity after a fast first paint.

definition: React components that run only on the server, read data directly and send serialised UI to the client without shipping their code.
details: Client Components (`'use client'`) handle interactivity; props crossing the boundary must be serialisable.
Server Actions/Functions are public endpoints — validate and authorise every call.
Reduce client JavaScript and request waterfalls.
useCases: Keeping secrets and heavy libraries off the client.

definition: A React mechanism that shows a fallback while part of the UI waits for code or data, and enables streaming server rendering.
details: Place boundaries around meaningful UI regions, paired with error boundaries.
Transitions keep the old UI visible during non-urgent updates instead of flashing fallbacks.
Data must come from Suspense-enabled sources (frameworks, libraries, `use()`).

definition: Updating the UI immediately as if a mutation succeeded, then confirming with the server or rolling back on failure.
details: Snapshot, apply, send with an idempotency key, then confirm or roll back.
Cancel in-flight refetches that could overwrite the optimistic state.
Avoid for risky actions such as payments.

definition: A data structure that lets replicas be edited independently and concurrently and then merged automatically without conflicts.
details: Libraries include Yjs and Automerge.
Powers offline-first apps and real-time collaborative editing.
Trade-offs: metadata overhead and limited fit for strict business invariants.

definition: A background thread in the browser (or Node worker thread) that runs JavaScript in parallel with the main thread, communicating by messages.
details: Keeps the main thread free for input and rendering.
Data is copied (structured clone) unless transferred (ArrayBuffers).
Shared memory needs SharedArrayBuffer and cross-origin isolation.
useCases: Parsing large files, image processing, heavy filtering.

definition: The modern React Native internals that replace the asynchronous JSON bridge with JSI (direct JS–native calls), the Fabric renderer and lazily loaded, typed TurboModules.
details: Enables React concurrent features and synchronous layout reads.
Codegen generates type-safe native interfaces from typed specs.
Third-party libraries must support it; check before upgrading.

definition: Shipping JavaScript and asset changes to installed mobile apps without a new app store release.
details: Runtime versions ensure updates only reach binaries with compatible native code.
Must follow store policies — no major new features bypassing review.
Roll out gradually and keep rollback ready.
useCases: Small content and UI changes between store releases.

definition: Attributes that add roles, states and properties to the accessibility tree when native HTML can't express a widget's semantics.
details: First rule: don't use ARIA if a native element does the job.
ARIA changes semantics only — keyboard behaviour must still be implemented.
Follow the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices patterns for tabs, comboboxes and menus.
useCases: Disclosure buttons (`aria-expanded`) and live status messages.
